title: Where Am I?
brief: Use the `pwd` command to print the directory you are standing in.

hints.text: Type `pwd` (Present Working Directory) and press Enter.

successMessage: You are at /home/analyst. `pwd` always prints your absolute location in the directory tree.

title: Survey the Ground
brief: Use `ls` to list the files and directories where you are standing.

hints.text: Type `ls` to list files and folders.

successMessage: `ls` lists directory contents. You can see Documents, Downloads, evidence, training, and welcome.txt.

title: Hidden in Plain Sight
brief: Something is hiding in your home directory. In Linux, files beginning with `.` are invisible to a plain `ls`. Use `ls -la` to find `.stash`, then read it with `cat .stash`. Submit the captured flag.

hints.text: Run `ls -la` or `ls -a` to reveal files starting with a dot (`.`).
Run `cat .stash` to read the hidden file, then submit the recovered flag.

successMessage: Dotfiles like `.bashrc` and `.stash` are hidden by default. In cyber forensics, malware and adversaries frequently disguise payloads as dotfiles.

title: One Level Down
brief: Move into `training/level_1`. Read `checkpoint_alpha.txt` and submit the recovered flag.

hints.text: Use `cd training/level_1` to move down into it.
Once inside level_1, run `cat checkpoint_alpha.txt` to view the flag.

successMessage: `cd` changes your working directory. You navigated down through child directory `training` into `level_1`.

title: Sideways Move
brief: Now reach `training/level_2` — a SIBLING of level_1, not a child. If you are inside level_1, you must go up before you can go over. Read `checkpoint_beta.txt` and submit the flag.

hints.text: A sibling directory is reached by going UP first, then over. From your home directory the whole trip is one command: `cd training/level_2`.
Once you are inside, run `cat checkpoint_beta.txt` and submit the flag.

successMessage: `..` represents the parent directory. `cd ..` moves you up one level toward the root.
commandCheckExemptReason: Hint is conditional on already being inside level_1; the absolute-path alternative is verified instead.

title: Warp Speed (Tab Completion)
brief: Typing full directory paths is slow. Type `cd Doc` and press Tab to auto-complete `cd Documents`, then press Enter.

hints.text: Type `cd Doc` then press the Tab key. The shell will auto-complete to `cd Documents`.

successMessage: Tab completion prevents typos and speeds up navigation. In incident response, Tab is indispensable.
commandCheckExemptReason: Intentionally incomplete prefix — the challenge is to press Tab to complete it.

title: Recall the Past (History)
brief: Your recent commands are saved. Press the Up Arrow key to bring back a command you ran earlier — like `pwd` — then press Enter.

hints.text: Run `pwd`, then press Up Arrow and Enter.

successMessage: Up/Down arrows cycle through your command history. Combined with Tab completion, you can operate the terminal with rapid precision.

title: Read the Case File
brief: Every investigation starts by opening the case file. Display `Documents/case_notes.txt` on screen using `cat`.

hints.text: `cat` takes the path to the file you want printed.
Run `cat Documents/case_notes.txt`.

successMessage: `cat` concatenates and prints entire file contents. Great for dossiers, configurations, and small text files.

title: The Earliest Anomaly
brief: `Documents/access.log` holds a long record. Show only its first 5 entries using `head`.

hints.text: `head` prints the top of a file. One flag sets how many lines.
Run `head -n 5 Documents/access.log`.

successMessage: `head` outputs the start of a file (default 10 lines). `-n 5` restricts it to the first 5 records.

title: The Sensor Freeze
brief: The incident happened right before the sensors went dark, so the evidence is at the END of `Documents/access.log`. Read the final entries and submit the flag.

hints.text: `tail` prints the bottom of a file, the opposite end from `head`.
Run `tail Documents/access.log`, then submit the flag on the last line.

successMessage: `tail` displays the final lines of a file. In live forensics, `tail -f` streams incoming logs in real-time.

title: Don't Trust Extensions
brief: Never trust a filename — an analyst identifies a file by its contents. Determine the true format of `evidence/mystery_file`.

hints.text: One command reads a file's magic bytes and reports what it really is.
Run `file evidence/mystery_file`.

successMessage: The `file` command examines file signatures (magic bytes). Never assume a file is safe or text based on its extension!

title: Carving Binary Artifacts
brief: `evidence/binary_data` is a compiled executable, so `cat` gives you garbage. Pull the readable text out of it and submit the flag hidden inside.

hints.text: One command extracts printable character sequences from a binary.
Run `strings evidence/binary_data`, then submit the recovery token in the output.

successMessage: `strings` extracts 4+ character ASCII/printable strings from binaries, memory dumps, and corrupt files. It is standard for malware triage.

title: Integrity Checksum (MD5)
brief: Digital evidence must be hashed to prove nobody altered it. Compute the MD5 hash of `evidence/evidence.img`, then read the image header to find and submit the acquisition flag.

hints.text: One command computes an MD5 digest. Reading the header afterwards is a plain `cat`.
Run `md5sum evidence/evidence.img`, then `cat evidence/evidence.img`.

successMessage: Always hash evidence upon acquisition and before/after examination to prove the forensic image was not altered.

title: Secrets in Plain Sight
brief: `Documents/secrets.txt` is long, and only one line matters. Find the line containing `vault_passcode` and submit the flag on it.

hints.text: `grep` searches a file for a pattern. Give it the pattern first, then the file.
Run `grep vault_passcode Documents/secrets.txt`.

successMessage: `grep` searches files for matching text strings. It is one of the most powerful utilities in the Unix ecosystem.

title: Case-Insensitive Searching
brief: `Documents/logs.txt` records errors inconsistently as 'error', 'ERROR' and 'Error'. Find every error line with a single search, then submit the flag one of them carries.

hints.text: One short `grep` flag makes the match ignore letter case.
Run `grep -i "error" Documents/logs.txt`.

successMessage: `grep -i` ignores case distinctions, making it essential when analyzing unstructured application logs.

title: Needle in /var/log
brief: Log files are scattered somewhere under `/var/log`. List every file there whose name ends in `.log`, then read the sensor audit log and submit the keycode flag.

hints.text: `find` walks a directory tree, and it can filter on the filename. Quote the wildcard pattern.
Run `find /var/log -name "*.log"`, then `cat /var/log/sensor_audit.log`.

successMessage: `find` traverses entire directory hierarchies searching by filename patterns, file types, timestamps, and sizes.

title: The WSL Bridge
brief: This machine has a Windows side mounted at `/mnt/c`. Read the intake sheet at `/mnt/c/Users/analyst/Desktop/CASE_FILES/intake.txt` and submit the flag.

hints.text: WSL mounts each Windows drive under `/mnt`, so drive C: appears as `/mnt/c`.
Run `cat /mnt/c/Users/analyst/Desktop/CASE_FILES/intake.txt`.

successMessage: That is the WSL bridge: `C:\Users\x` on Windows maps to `/mnt/c/Users/x` in Linux.

title: The Bridge, Unassisted
brief: A second dossier sits on the Windows side at `C:\Users\analyst\Documents\surface_notes.txt`. Reach it from this Linux shell and submit the flag inside. Nobody will translate the path for you.

hints.text: Translate the Windows path yourself: `C:\` becomes `/mnt/c/`, and every backslash becomes a forward slash.
Run `cat /mnt/c/Users/analyst/Documents/surface_notes.txt`.

successMessage: You translated a Windows path to its WSL location without a map.

title: Consult the Manual
brief: The `tracker` sensor suite has an undocumented manual override code, but it is written in the tool's own manual page. Read the manual, find the code, and submit it.

hints.text: Every serious Linux tool ships a manual page. One command opens it.
Run `man tracker` and read the DESCRIPTION section.

successMessage: `man` renders standard UNIX manual documentation.

title: Deploy the Sensor Suite (apt-get)
brief: The `tracker` tool is not installed on this machine. Install it from the package repository, then run a sensor sweep with it and submit the flag.

hints.text: Refresh the package lists first, then install. Both steps need administrator rights. The sweep flag for `tracker` is `-a`.
Run `sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install tracker -y`, then `tracker -a`.

successMessage: `apt-get` is Debian/Ubuntu's package management suite.

title: Filter the Noise (Inverted Grep)
brief: `Documents/network_stream.log` is almost entirely normal `ALLOW` traffic. Show only the packets that are NOT allowed, and submit the flag on the CRITICAL_DATA_LEAK entry.

hints.text: `grep` normally keeps the matching lines. One flag inverts that and keeps everything else.
Run `grep -v "ALLOW" Documents/network_stream.log`.

successMessage: `grep -v` inverts matches, displaying all lines that do NOT match the pattern.

title: First Pipeline (grep | wc -l)
brief: You now know how to isolate the non-`ALLOW` packets in `Documents/network_stream.log`. This time do not read them — count them, in a single line, without writing anything to a file.

hints.text: The `|` operator feeds one command's output straight into the next. `wc -l` counts lines.
Run `grep -v "ALLOW" Documents/network_stream.log | wc -l`.

successMessage: The pipe `|` sends the output of `grep` into the input of `wc -l`. You constructed your first pipeline!

title: Extracting Fields (cut & grep)
brief: `Documents/security_events.csv` is comma separated. The rows tagged `FLAG_EMIT` carry a token in column 6. Isolate those rows, extract just that column, and submit the token.

hints.text: Two commands joined by a pipe: `grep` selects the rows, `cut` selects the column. `cut` needs the delimiter and the field number.
Run `grep "FLAG_EMIT" Documents/security_events.csv | cut -d, -f6`.

successMessage: Combining `grep` with `cut -d, -f<N>` lets you slice columns out of structured logs without complex spreadsheets.

title: Output Redirection (>)
brief: Pull every error line out of `Documents/logs.txt` and save them into a new file at `/tmp/errors.log` instead of printing them. Then read that file back to confirm it worked.

hints.text: `>` sends output into a file rather than the screen. Remember the flag that makes the search ignore case.
Run `grep -i "error" Documents/logs.txt > /tmp/errors.log`, then `cat /tmp/errors.log`.

successMessage: Redirection `>` writes stdout directly into the filesystem.

title: Partition Geometry Inspection
brief: `evidence/suspect_drive.raw` is a raw disk image. Analyze its partition table with the `scan` tool and note the starting sector offset of the Evidence Vault partition. You will need that number next.

hints.text: `scan` takes the path to the image.
Run `scan evidence/suspect_drive.raw` and read the Start Sector Offset it reports.

successMessage: The partition table identifies partition 2 (Evidence Vault) beginning at sector offset 206848.

title: Carve the Evidence (Finish Line)
brief: Carve the Evidence Vault partition out of `evidence/suspect_drive.raw` with the `extract` tool. It needs the sector offset you recovered in the partition scan — go back and read it if you did not write it down. Submit the Master Capstone Flag it decrypts.

hints.text: `extract` takes the offset with the `-o` flag, then the image path. The offset came from the `scan` output; the tool rejects a wrong one.
Run `extract -o 206848 evidence/suspect_drive.raw`, then submit the master flag it prints.

successMessage: Congratulations, Analyst! You read partition geometry, carried an offset from one tool into another, and carved out the master evidence.

title: Windows Navigation (dir & cd)
brief: You are now on the Windows side. List the files in `C:\Users\Analyst` using the Windows equivalent of `ls`.

hints.text: In cmd.exe the listing command is `dir`. On its own, `cd` prints where you are.
Run `dir`.

successMessage: `dir` is the Windows equivalent of `ls`. Notice Windows paths use backslashes.

title: Hidden File Attributes (attrib)
brief: Windows hides files with an attribute flag, not with a leading dot. Inspect the attributes of `evidence\mystery_file`, then read it and recover the flag.

hints.text: `attrib` shows a file's attribute letters; H means Hidden. `type` prints a file, the way `cat` does on Linux.
Run `attrib evidence\mystery_file`, then `type evidence\mystery_file`.

successMessage: `attrib` displays and modifies file attributes: R=Read-only, H=Hidden, S=System, A=Archive.

title: Windows String Search (findstr /i)
brief: Search the Windows event log at `Documents\logs.txt` for the flagged event containing `marker`, ignoring letter case, and submit the flag. Windows does not have `grep`.

hints.text: The cmd.exe search command is `findstr`. Its switches start with a forward slash, and `/i` ignores case.
Run `findstr /i "marker" Documents\logs.txt`.

successMessage: `findstr /i` is the Windows CMD equivalent of `grep -i`.

title: CertUtil Hashing
brief: Compute the MD5 hash of `evidence\evidence.img` for the chain of custody. Windows has no `md5sum`; the built-in tool for this is `certutil`.

hints.text: `certutil` needs the `-hashfile` switch, then the file, then the algorithm name.
Run `certutil -hashfile evidence\evidence.img MD5`.

successMessage: `certutil -hashfile` supports MD5, SHA1, and SHA256 without needing third-party utilities on Windows workstations.
